Why does excavating an artificial cavity cause settlement?
The original state of stress changes, and the ground above and beside it moves towards the cavity
Because the air in the cavity compresses the soil
Excavating a cavity changes the state of stress; the ground moves towards the cavity, and a settlement trough forms at the surface.
At what angle to the horizontal does the rupture surface run up from the lower corner of the cavity?
The rupture surfaces run up to the surface at about 45° + φ/2 to the horizontal, and they mark the width of the trough.
What does the magnitude of settlement approximately depend on?
On the volume of soil squeezed into the cavity
On the colour of the building
On the age of the cavity
The volume of the surface trough is approximately equal to the volume of soil squeezed into the cavity.
How do depth and soil strength affect the displacement?
With a deeper cavity and stronger soil, the displacement is smaller and occurs later
A deeper cavity always gives more settlement
In stronger soil it collapses at once
The deeper the cavity and the stronger the soil, the smaller and the later the displacement.
What should be done if a cavity is found under a building?
Support or backfill it as soon as possible, and keep it dry by dewatering
Wait until it collapses by itself
Strengthen the roof of the building
The cavity must be supported (or backfilled) and dewatered as soon as possible.
What does volume loss mean in tunnelling?
The volume of the surface trough as a percentage of the tunnel cross-section
The mass of soil carted away

Where does a house tilt the most in a settlement trough?
At the edge of the trough, near the inflection point
Exactly in the middle of the trough
At the inflection point (x = i) the trough is steepest; this is where tilt and tensile strain are greatest.
Why is it dangerous if a cellar cut into tuff becomes soaked?
The strength of the tuff drops to a fraction when saturated, and the vault may collapse
Because the water freezes in it in summer
Because tuff dissolves in water like salt
In Eger the strength of rhyodacite tuff drops to a third to a fifth when soaked – this is why rainwater and utility pipes must be routed away.
individual shocks < 1 s, in delayed sequences
up to 100 mm/s near the source
A short, sharp shock with a wide frequency band. In quarries and demolition; its effect is governed by the charge mass and the distance.
blows of about 0.2 s, every second
Each blow is a short impulse. It compacts loose sand around the pile; for the neighbouring building it is the many thousands of repetitions that are dangerous.
Driving sheet piles and piles with a vibrator. At start-up and shutdown the system passes through its natural frequency – that is when the vibration is strongest.
Heavy vehicles, trams, railways. Small-amplitude vibration, but repeated for decades; stronger on uneven surfacing and loose ground.
ten to sixty seconds of strong shaking
several hundred mm/s in a strong earthquake
Low-frequency, large-amplitude motion – right at the natural frequencies of buildings and soil layers. That is why it is the most dangerous dynamic effect.
Very low-frequency, slow gusts. They move tall, slender structures such as towers and wind turbines, and apply a cyclically alternating overturning moment to the foundation.
No numerical band is given for wind vibration. The frequency ranges are typical values; earthquakes fall right in the band of the natural frequencies of buildings and soil layers.
Cohesive soil is held together by cohesion; vibration hardly rearranges it.
Well-graded grains interlock, and the skeleton is dense to begin with.
Vibration rearranges the grains of the loose skeleton of uniform grains into a denser arrangement; the water pressure rises in the saturated pores.
When dry the risk is smaller, but loose, uniform sand still compacts.
The sweep changes the excitation like a vibrator starting up or a machine spinning up.
Even a small excitation causes a large amplitude. On loose, saturated soil sudden, collapse-like settlement is expected – the excitation must be detuned.
When vibrators start up and shut down, the system passes through this band – that is when the vibration is briefly stronger.
The system follows the excitation almost as a rigid body; there is no amplification.
The mass “cannot keep up” with the rapid excitation, and the amplitude is smaller than the static one. This is why a high frequency (≥ 1.5 × f0) is chosen for vibratory driving.
